passage_1.text:
In the summer of 2022, subscribers to the US streaming service HBO MAX were alarmed to discover that dozens of the platform's offerings from the Covid-themed heist thriller Locked Down to the recent remake of The Witches – had been quietly removed from the service. The news seemed like vindication to those who had long warned that streaming was more about controlling access to the cultural commons than expanding it, as did reports (since denied by the show's creators) that Netflix had begun editing old episodes of Stranger Things to retroactively improve their visual effects.

What's less clear is whether the commonly prescribed cure for these cultural ills – a return to the material pleasures of physical media – is the right one. While the makers of Blu-ray discs claim they have a shelf life of 100 years, such statistics remain largely theoretical until they come to pass, and are dependent on storage conditions, not to mention the continued availability of playback equipment. The humble DVD has already proved far less resilient, with many early releases already beginning to deteriorate in quality. Digital movie purchases provide even less security. Any film "bought" on iTunes could disappear if you move to another territory with a different rights agreement and try to redownload it. It's a bold new frontier in the commodification of art: the birth of the product recall. After a man took to Twitter to bemoan losing access to Cars 2 after moving from Canada to Australia, Apple clarified that users who downloaded films to their devices would retain permanent access to those downloads, even if they relocated to a hemisphere where the content was subject to a different set of rights agreements. Thanks to the company's ironclad digital rights management technology, however, such files cannot be moved or backed up, locking you into watching with your Apple account.

Anyone who does manage to acquire Digital Rights Management free (DRM-free) copies of their favourite films must nonetheless grapple with ever-changing file format standards, not to mention data decay – the gradual process by which electronic information slowly but surely corrupts. Only the regular migration of files from hard drive to hard drive can delay the inevitable, in a Sisyphean battle against the ravages of digital time.

In a sense, none of this is new. Charlie Chaplin burned the negative of his 1926 film A Woman of the Sea as a tax write-off. Many more films have been lost through accident, negligence or plain indifference. During a heat wave in July 1937, a Fox film vault in New Jersey burned down, destroying a majority of the silent films produced by the studio.

Back then, at least, cinema was defined by its ephemerality: the sense that a film was as good as gone once it left your local cinema. Today, with film studios keen to stress the breadth of their back catalogues (or to put in Hollywood terms, the value of their IPs), audiences may start to wonder why those same studios seem happy to set the vault alight themselves if it'll help next quarter's numbers.

passage_4.text:
The idea of craftsmanship is not simply nostalgic. Crafts require distinct skills, an all-round approach to work that involves the whole product, rather than individual parts, and an attitude that necessitates devotion to the job and a focus on the communal interest. The concept of craft emphasises the human touch and individual judgment.

Essentially, the crafts concept seems to run against the preponderant ethos of management studies which, as the academics note, have long prioritised efficiency and consistency. Craft skills were portrayed as being primitive and traditionalist.

The contrast between artisanship and efficiency first came to the fore in the 19 century when British manufacturers suddenly faced competition from across the Atlantic as firms developed the “American system” using standardised parts. The worldwide success of the Singer sewing machine showed the potential of a mass-produced device. This process created its own reaction, first in the form of the Arts and Crafts movement of the late 19th century, and then again in the “small is beautiful' movement of the 1970s. A third crafts movement is emerging as people become aware of the environmental impact of conventional industry.

There are two potential markets for those who practise crafts. The first stems from the existence of consumers who are willing to pay a premium price for goods that are deemed to be of extra quality. The second market lies in those consumers who wish to use their purchases to support local workers, or to reduce their environmental impact by taking goods to craftspeople to be mended, or recycled.

For workers, the appeal of craftsmanship is that it allows them the autonomy to make creative choices, and thus makes a job far more satisfying. In that sense, it could offer hope for the overall labour market. Let the machines automate dull and repetitive tasks and let workers focus purely on their skills, judgment and imagination. As a current example, the academics cite the “agile” manifesto in the software sector, an industry at the heart of technological change. The pioneers behind the original agile manifesto promised to prioritise "individuals and interactions over processes and tools". By bringing together experts from different teams, agile working is designed to improve creativity.

But the broader question is whether crafts can create a lot more jobs than they do today. Demand for crafted products may rise but will it be easy to retrain workers in sectors that might get automated (such as truck drivers) to take advantage? In a world where products and services often have to pass through regulatory hoops, large companies will usually have the advantage.

History also suggests that the link between crafts and creativity is not automatic. Medieval craft guilds were monopolies which resisted new entrants. They were also highly hierarchical with young men required to spend long periods as apprentices and journeymen before they could set up on their own; by that time the innovative spirit may have been knocked out of them. Craft workers can thrive in the modern era, but only if they don't get too organised.

passage_6.text:
Landing in Australia, the British colonists weren't much impressed with the small-bodied, slender-snooted marsupials called bandicoots. “Their muzzle, which is much too long, gives them an air exceedingly stupid," one naturalist noted in 1805. They nicknamed one type the “zebra rat' because of its black-striped rump.

Silly-looking or not, though, the zebra rat—the smallest bandicoot, more commonly known today as the western barred bandicoot—exhibited a genius for survival in the harsh outback, where its ancestors had persisted for some 26 million years. Its births were triggered by rainfall in the bone-dry desert. It carried its breath-mint-size babies in a backward-facing pouch so mothers could forage for food and dig shallow, camouflaged shelters.

Still, these adaptations did not prepare the western barred bandicoot for the colonial-era transformation of its ecosystem, particularly the onslaught of imported British animals, from cattle and rabbits that damaged delicate desert vegetation to ravenous house cats that soon developed a taste for bandicoots. Several of the dozen-odd bandicoot species went extinct, and by the 1940s the western barred bandicoot, whose original range stretched across much of the continent, persisted only on two predator-free islands in Shark Bay, off Australia's western coast.

“Our isolated fauna had simply not been exposed to these predators,” says Reece Pedler, an ecologist with the Wild Deserts conservation program.

Now Wild Deserts is using descendants of those few thousand island survivors, called Shark Bay bandicoots, in a new effort to seed a mainland bandicoot revival. They've imported 20 bandicoots to a preserve on the edge of the Strzelecki Desert, in the remote interior of New South Wales. This sanctuary is a challenging place, desolate much of the year, with one of the world's most mercurial rainfall patterns—relentless droughts followed by sudden drenching floods.

The imported bandicoots occupy two fenced “exclosures,” cleared of invasive rabbits (courtesy of Pedler's sheepdog) and of feral cats (which slunk off once the rabbits disappeared). A third fenced area contains the program's Wild Training Zone, where two other rare marsupials (bilbies, a larger type of bandicoot, and mulgaras, a somewhat fearsome fuzzball known for sucking the brains out of prey) currently share terrain with controlled numbers of cats, learning to evade them. It's unclear whether the Shark Bay bandicoots, which are perhaps even more predator-naive than their now-extinct mainland bandicoot kin, will be able to make that kind of breakthrough.

For now, though, a recent surge of rainfall has led to a bandicoot joey boom, raising the Wild Deserts population to about 100, with other sanctuaries adding to that number. There are also signs of rebirth in the landscape itself. With their constant digging, the bandicoots trap moisture and allow for seed germination so the cattle-damaged desert can restore itself.

They have a new nickname—a flattering one, this time. “We call them ecosystem engineers,” Pedler says.

passage_8.text:
Oftentimes, when economists cross borders, they are less interested in learning from others than in invading their garden plots. Gary Becker, for instance, pioneered the idea of human capital. To do so, he famously tackled topics like crime and domesticity, applying methods honed in the study of markets to domains of nonmarket life. He projected economics outward into new realms: for example, by revealing the extent to which humans calculate marginal utilities when choosing their spouses or stealing from neighbors. At the same time, he did not let other ways of thinking enter his own economic realm: for example, he did not borrow from anthropology or history or let observations of nonmarket economics inform his homo economicus. Becker was a picture of the imperial economist in the heyday of the discipline’s bravura.

Times have changed for the once almighty discipline. Economics has been taken to task, within and beyond its ramparts. Some economists have reached out, imported, borrowed, and collaborated—been less imperial, more open. Consider Thomas Piketty and his outreach to historians. The booming field of behavioral economics—the fusion of economics and social psychology—is another case. Having spawned active subfields, like judgment, decision-making and a turn to experimentation, the field aims to go beyond the caricature of Rational Man to explain how humans make decisions.

It is important to underscore how this flips the way we think about economics. For generations, economists have presumed that people have interests—‘preferences,” in the neoclassical argot—that get revealed in the course of peoples’ choices. Interests come before actions and determine them. If you are hungry, you buy lunch; if you are cold, you get a sweater. If you only have so much money and can't afford to deal with both your growling stomach and your shivering, which need you choose to meet using your scarce savings reveals your preference.

Psychologists take one look at this simple formulation and shake their heads. Increasingly, even some mainstream economists have to admit that homo economicus doesn’t always behave like the textbook maximizer; irrational behavior can’t simply be waved away as extra-economic expressions of passions over interests, and thus the domain of other disciplines... .This is one place where the humanist can help the economist. If narrative economics is going to help us understand how rivals duke it out, who wins and who loses, we are going to need much more than lessons from epidemiological studies of viruses or intracranial stimuli.

Above all, we need politics and institutions. Shiller (the Nobel Prize–winning economist) connects perceptions of narratives to changes in behavior and thence to social outcomes. He completes a circle that was key to behavioral economics and brings in storytelling to make sense of how perceptions get framed. This cycle (perception to behavior to society) was once mediated or dominated by institutions: the political parties, lobby groups, and media organizations that played a vital role in legitimating, representing, and excluding interests. Yet institutions have been stripped from Shiller's account, to reveal a bare dynamic of emotions and economics, without the intermediating place of politics.

questions.question_text: "Netflix had begun editing old episodes of Stranger Things to retroactively improve their visual effects." What is the purpose of this example used in the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: To show that art in the digital age, specifically film, is no longer sacrosanct, and may be changed to suit changing tastes or technology.

options.label: B
options.text: To show that streaming services are controlling access to the cultural commons rather than expanding it.

options.label: C
options.text: To show how unsubstantiated reports are leading to an increase in the level of distrust towards streaming services.

options.label: D
options.text: To show a practice that justifies the fears of people who feel streaming services cannot be trusted to be custodians of cultural artefacts like film.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the specific purpose of the Stranger Things example in the passage's argument.

From passage: "The news seemed like vindication to those who had long warned that streaming was more about controlling access to the cultural commons than expanding it, as did reports (since denied by the show's creators) that Netflix had begun editing old episodes of Stranger Things to retroactively improve their visual effects."

The key word here is "vindication" -> this means proof that someone was right. The author is saying both the HBO Max removals AND the Stranger Things editing served as vindication -> they proved that people who already had concerns were correct.

So the thought process is: Some people already worried about streaming services -> These incidents happened -> These incidents validated/justified those pre-existing worries.

Elimination Process:

🟠 Option 1 -> scope-error -> talks about "art in digital age" generally, but the passage uses this example specifically to validate concerns about streaming services as custodians, not just about digital art changing

🟠 Option 2 -> context-shift -> mentions "controlling cultural commons" which is the broader theme the passage discusses, but not the specific purpose of the Stranger Things example within that theme

🟠 Option 3 -> misinterprets -> says "unsubstantiated reports leading to distrust" but the passage presents these as evidence supporting existing concerns, not as creating baseless distrust

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> perfectly matches "vindication to those who had long warned" -> the example justifies the fears of people who already didn't trust streaming services as reliable preservers of cultural works

The confusion students often have is between Options 2 and 4. Option 2 talks about the big picture theme, while Option 4 talks about the specific job this example does within that theme -> it provides evidence to back up existing worries.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements, if true, would best invalidate the main argument of the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Improved cloud storage services have made it possible for movie collections to now be preserved in perpetuity, without the need to keep migrating the files.

options.label: B
options.text: When moving to a different geographical location, customers can easily use Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) to bypass geo-blocking and regain access to their content on any streaming service.

options.label: C
options.text: Recent research has irrefutably proven that Blu-Ray discs have a shelf life of at least 100years.

options.label: D
options.text: Studios and streaming services have committed to giving customers perpetual, platform-independent access to their content.

questions.explanation_text:
To solve this, we need to first identify the main argument of the passage, then find which option would completely tear it down.

The passage's core argument: Digital media gives users less control and permanence than they think -> streaming services control access rather than expand it -> content gets removed -> you don't really "own" digital purchases -> DRM locks you into platforms.

From passage: "The news seemed like vindication to those who had long warned that streaming was more about controlling access to the cultural commons than expanding it"

The passage argues digital media has major problems: content removal -> geo-blocking -> platform dependence -> data decay -> format changes. All of these show users lack real control over their digital content.

Now we need to find which option would completely destroy this argument, not just address one small part.

Students often get confused between options that fix one problem vs options that fix the core issue.

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> fixes data decay/migration but ignores content removal, DRM, platform control. The passage says digital media has multiple problems - fixing just one doesn't invalidate the whole argument.

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> VPNs help with geo-blocking when you move countries, but streaming services can still remove shows, you're still locked into platforms with DRM. Again, fixes one issue but leaves the main argument intact.

🔴 Option 3 -> opposite-direction -> this actually supports the passage! If Blu-rays last 100 years, that makes physical media look even better compared to problematic digital media. This strengthens the passage's argument instead of invalidating it.

🟢 Option 4 -> directly attacks core argument -> if studios gave "perpetual, platform-independent access," this would eliminate content removal, geo-blocking, platform dependence, and DRM issues all at once. This would mean digital media actually does expand access rather than control it, completely invalidating the passage's main point.

The key insight: Options 1-2 only fix symptoms, but Option 4 fixes the disease itself.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about art best captures the arguments made in the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: In the age of online subscription services, it is time to change our understanding of classic works of art being primarily immutable and easily available to the public.

options.label: B
options.text: Accepting retroactive changes to works of art is dangerous because it will encourage creators to not put enough effort into the original attempt, given that they can always edit or update their work later.

options.label: C
options.text: Works of art belong to the cultural commons and hence must remain available in perpetuity, irrespective of who pays for access to them.

options.label: D
options.text: As art is increasingly created, stored and distributed digitally, access to it is counter intuitively likely to be made more difficult by the rapid churn in technology and the whims of host platforms.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage starts with HBO Max removing content -> discusses problems with both physical and digital media -> concludes that despite promising more access, digital platforms actually make art less accessible due to their control and technological changes.

From passage: "The news seemed like vindication to those who had long warned that streaming was more about controlling access to the cultural commons than expanding it"

From passage: "It's a bold new frontier in the commodification of art: the birth of the product recall"

Thought process:

Streaming promised more access -> but actually gives platforms more control -> physical media has problems too -> digital files face format changes and decay -> this makes art paradoxically harder to access despite better technology

Elimination strategy:

Look for the option that captures the paradox - better technology should mean better access, but actually makes it worse.

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> talks about "changing our understanding" but passage isn't about changing perspectives, it's about describing current problems with access

🔴 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> only mentions the Netflix editing point (tiny part of passage) but completely ignores the main argument about access difficulties

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> passage doesn't argue what art "should" be or ownership philosophy, just describes current access problems with platforms

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> perfectly captures the central paradox: digital technology should make art more accessible, but platform control and tech changes actually make it counter-intuitively harder to access

The key insight is the word "counter-intuitively" in Option 4 - this captures exactly what the passage argues: we'd expect digital to improve access, but it actually makes it worse.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is suggested by the sentence “Back then, at least, cinema was defined by its ephemerality: the sense that a film was as good as gone once it left your local cinema”?

options.label: A
options.text: Today, films are expected to be available for a long time, since they are no longer tied solely to their stay at the local cinema.

options.label: B
options.text: Cinema is now no longer as ephemeral as it used to be earlier, because the technology used for creating and preserving films has improved manifold.

options.label: C
options.text: Presently, there is no reason why film studios should remove access to films once they have left the local cinema.

options.label: D
options.text: Around a century ago, people were more accepting of not having access to films once they left the local cinema.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Back then, at least, cinema was defined by its ephemerality: the sense that a film was as good as gone once it left your local cinema."

The key word here is "at least" -> this signals a contrast with today. The author is saying that in the past, people accepted that films would disappear after leaving cinemas, but things are different now.

The sentence structure: Past = ephemeral (temporary) vs. Present = implied permanence expected.

Elimination Strategy: Look for the option that captures both sides of this time contrast, not just one side.

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> correctly identifies past vs. present change but wrongly focuses on technology as the reason. The sentence doesn't mention technology at all.

🔴 Option 3 -> irrelevant -> makes a prescriptive statement about what studios "should" do. The sentence is descriptive about expectations, not giving advice.

🟠 Option 4 -> incomplete -> only talks about the past side (people were accepting) but misses the crucial contrast with today that the sentence implies.

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures both sides perfectly: today films are expected to be available long-term (opposite of ephemeral) because they're not tied to just cinema screenings anymore.

The sentence suggests that expectations have shifted from accepting temporary access to expecting permanent access.

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: A volume of translated Italian madrigals were published in London during the year of 1588. This sudden public interest facilitated a surge of English Madrigal writing as well as a spurt of other secular music writing and publication ___ (1) ___ . This music boom lasted for thirty years and was as much a golden age of music as British literature was with Shakespeare and Queen Elizabeth ___ (2) ___ . The rebirth in both literature and music originated in Italy and migrated to England; the English madrigal became more humorous and lighter in England as compared to Italy. Renaissance music was mostly polyphonic in texture ___ (3) ___ . Extreme use of and contrasts in dynamics, rhythm, and tone colour do not occur ___ (4) ___ . The rhythms in Renaissance music tend to have a smooth, soft flow instead of a sharp, well-defined pulse of accents.

Sentence: Comprehending a wide range of emotions, Renaissance music nevertheless portrayed all emotions in a balanced and moderate fashion.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 3

options.label: B
options.text: Option 4

options.label: C
options.text: Option 1

options.label: D
options.text: Option 2

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Renaissance music was mostly polyphonic in texture ___ (3) ___. Extreme use of and contrasts in dynamics, rhythm, and tone colour do not occur ___ (4) ___."

Thought Process:

First, check if Renaissance music is mentioned before each position -> Only positions 3 and 4 come after Renaissance music is introduced -> Now check logical flow -> Position 3 follows the introduction of Renaissance music -> Position 4 would break the connection between sentences about musical dynamics and rhythm.

Option Analysis:

🔴 Option 2 (Position 4): -> context-shift -> breaks the logical flow between two connected sentences about musical dynamics. The sentence before talks about no extreme contrasts and after talks about smooth rhythms - inserting our sentence disrupts this connection.

🔴 Option 3 (Position 1): -> scope-error -> Renaissance music hasn't been introduced yet, so talking about its emotional qualities makes no sense here.

🔴 Option 4 (Position 2): -> scope-error -> same problem as Option 3, Renaissance music still not introduced as a topic.

🟢 Option 1 (Position 3): -> correct placement -> comes right after Renaissance music was mostly polyphonic in texture, establishing the topic. The idea of balanced and moderate emotions perfectly sets up the next sentence about avoiding extreme contrasts.

Key Elimination Strategy: In sentence insertion questions, always check if the topic is properly introduced before the position. Here, positions 1 and 2 fail because Renaissance music isn't mentioned yet. Position 4 fails because it breaks logical flow between connected ideas.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Cartographers design and create maps to communicate information about phenomena located somewhere on our planet. In the past, cartographers did not worry too much about who was going to read their maps. Although some simple “usability” research was done—like comparing whether circle or bar symbols worked best cartographers knew how to make maps. This has changed now, however, due to all kinds of societal and technological developments. Today, map readers are more demanding mostly because of the tools they use to read maps. Cartographers, who are also influenced by these trends, are now more interested in seeing if their products are efficient, effective, and appreciated.

options.label: A
options.text: Maps are being used for a variety of reasons and therefore map readers have become more demanding.

options.label: B
options.text: Today, cartographers also need to look into the usability of maps because of the new technological developments.

options.label: C
options.text: New technological developments have prompted cartographers to experiment with their maps by applying these new innovations.

options.label: D
options.text: Modern mapmakers evaluate a map's effectiveness efficiency and satisfaction of the user through a series of experiments.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the main shift that happened in cartography and what caused it.

From passage: "This has changed now, however, due to all kinds of societal and technological developments. Today, map readers are more demanding mostly because of the tools they use to read maps."

The passage shows a clear before vs after picture:

  • Past: Cartographers didn't worry much about who read their maps
  • Present: They now care about efficiency, effectiveness, and user satisfaction

Key cause -> technological developments made readers more demanding -> cartographers must focus on usability

Elimination Process:

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> says "variety of reasons" but passage focuses on technological tools making readers demanding, not variety of uses

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> captures both the usability focus AND the technological cause perfectly

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> talks about "experimenting with innovations" but passage is about user-focused design, not applying new tech to maps

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> mentions evaluation methods but misses the cause (tech developments) and focuses too much on experiments which isn't the main point

Student confusion: You might think Option 4 sounds good because it mentions "effectiveness" and "efficiency" from the passage. But it's missing the why - the technological developments that caused this shift. Option 2 gives you both the what changed (usability focus) and why it changed (tech developments).

questions.question_text: The author questions the ability of crafts to create substantial employment opportunities presently because

options.label: A
options.text: crafts guilds tend to resist new entrants and are unlikely to accept large numbers of trainees.

options.label: B
options.text: regulatory requirements could make it difficult for small crafts outfits to compete.

options.label: C
options.text: workers made redundant by automation are unlikely to opt for crafts-related work.

options.label: D
options.text: the low scale of crafts production will not be able to absorb the mass of redundant labour.

questions.explanation_text:
Need to find the current challenges mentioned, not historical ones.

From passage: "But the broader question is whether crafts can create a lot more jobs than they do today... In a world where products and services often have to pass through regulatory hoops, large companies will usually have the advantage."

The author's concern -> small craft businesses face regulatory challenges -> big companies have advantages -> harder for crafts to compete -> limits job creation potential.

Students often get confused between options 2 and 4 since both seem to address capacity issues. Here's how to eliminate:

🟠 Option 1 -> context-shift -> mentions guild resistance but this is about medieval history, not current employment challenges

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> directly matches the passage's point about regulatory barriers giving big companies advantages over small craft businesses

🟠 Option 3 -> misreads passage -> passage asks if it will be easy to retrain workers, doesn't say they're unwilling to switch

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> while scale might be implied, the passage specifically highlights regulatory hoops as the main barrier, not production scale itself

Key elimination tip: Look for current challenges the author mentions, not historical examples or assumptions not stated in the passage.

questions.question_text: We can infer from the passage that medieval crafts guilds resembled mass production in that both

options.label: A
options.text: focused excessively on product quality.

options.label: B
options.text: discouraged innovation by restricting entry through strict rules.

options.label: C
options.text: did not necessarily promote creativity.

options.label: D
options.text: did not always employ egalitarian production processes.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what medieval craft guilds and mass production had in common based on the passage.

From passage: "Medieval craft guilds were monopolies which resisted new entrants. They were also highly hierarchical with young men required to spend long periods as apprentices and journeymen before they could set up on their own; by that time the innovative spirit may have been knocked out of them."

From passage: "Essentially, the crafts concept seems to run against the preponderant ethos of management studies which, as the academics note, have long prioritised efficiency and consistency."

The key insight -> Both systems ended up stifling creativity, just through different methods:

  • Craft guilds -> rigid hierarchy knocked out innovative spirit
  • Mass production -> focus on efficiency/consistency over creativity

Students often get confused between options 2 and 3 here. Eliminating:

🟠 Option 1 -> scope-error -> Passage doesn't say either system focused on quality. Mass production focused on efficiency/standardization, not quality

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> True for craft guilds (monopolies resisting entrants) but mass production doesn't restrict entry the same way. This only describes one system

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> Both systems failed to promote creativity. Craft guilds knocked out "innovative spirit" through hierarchy, mass production prioritized "efficiency and consistency" over individual creativity

🟠 Option 4 -> context-shift -> Both were hierarchical, but the passage's main comparison is about their impact on creativity, not hierarchy itself

The confusion between 2 and 3: Option 2 looks tempting because craft guilds did restrict entry, but remember -> the question asks what both systems did. Mass production doesn't restrict entry through strict rules the same way guilds did.

questions.question_text: The most recent revival in interest in the crafts is a result of the emergence of all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: support for individual creations as opposed to mass-produced objects.

options.label: B
options.text: a niche market for discerning buyers of quality products.

options.label: C
options.text: a greater interest in buying locally produced goods.

options.label: D
options.text: concerns about the environmental impact of mass production.

questions.explanation_text:
Look for what's NOT mentioned as a cause of the recent crafts revival. Need to find what the passage actually says about the third/most recent movement.

From passage: "A third crafts movement is emerging as people become aware of the environmental impact of conventional industry."

From passage: "There are two potential markets for those who practise crafts. The first stems from the existence of consumers who are willing to pay a premium price for goods that are deemed to be of extra quality. The second market lies in those consumers who wish to use their purchases to support local workers, or to reduce their environmental impact..."

Process: Find what passage explicitly mentions -> Check each option against these mentions -> Pick the one NOT mentioned.

🟢 Option 2 -> explicitly mentioned -> "consumers willing to pay premium price for goods deemed to be of extra quality" = niche market for quality

🟢 Option 3 -> explicitly mentioned -> "consumers who wish to support local workers" = buying locally produced goods

🟢 Option 4 -> explicitly mentioned -> "people become aware of environmental impact" = environmental concerns driving revival

🔴 Option 1 -> not explicitly stated -> passage talks about crafts vs mass production historically (19th century Singer machines, etc.) but doesn't say recent revival is due to supporting individual creations over mass production

The confusion: Students might think Option 1 is correct because the passage discusses crafts vs mass production. But that discussion is historical context (19th century), not about what's driving the current revival.

The passage gives specific reasons for the recent movement -> environmental awareness, quality market, local support. "Individual vs mass production" isn't listed as a current motivator.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements is NOT inconsistent with the views stated in the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Creativity in the crafts could be stifled if the market for artisan goods becomes too organised.

options.label: B
options.text: The Arts and Crafts movement was initially inspired by the “American system" of production.

options.label: C
options.text: We need to support the crafts; only then can we retain the creativity intrinsic to their production.

options.label: D
options.text: The agile movement in software is a throwback to the tenets of the medieval crafts guilds.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which statement IS consistent with the passage (the double negative makes it tricky - "NOT inconsistent" means consistent).

From passage: "Medieval craft guilds were monopolies which resisted new entrants. They were also highly hierarchical... by that time the innovative spirit may have been knocked out of them. Craft workers can thrive in the modern era, but only if they don't get too organised."

The passage shows two key themes: crafts can boost creativity but over-organization kills that creativity.

From passage: "This process created its own reaction, first in the form of the Arts and Crafts movement of the late 19th century"

The Arts and Crafts movement was a reaction against the American system, not inspired by it.

Eliminating:

🔴 Option 2 -> factual-error -> Says Arts and Crafts was "inspired by" American system, but passage clearly says it was a "reaction" against it. Complete opposite meaning.

🔴 Option 4 -> context-shift -> Calls agile movement a "throwback" to medieval guilds, but passage contrasts them. Agile emphasizes creativity and collaboration while medieval guilds were hierarchical and stifled innovation.

🟠 Option 3 -> overstates -> Says crafts are the "only" way to retain creativity, but passage gives agile software as another example of creative work. Too absolute.

🟢 Option 1 -> perfectly matches -> Directly aligns with passage's warning that craft workers "can thrive... but only if they don't get too organised." Uses medieval guilds as historical proof that over-organization kills creativity.

The passage's main point: crafts can be creative unless they become too organized (like medieval guilds did).

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Scientific research shows that many animals are very intelligent and have sensory and motor abilities that dwarf ours. Dogs are able to detect diseases such as cancer and diabetes and warn humans of impending heart attacks and strokes. Elephants, whales, hippopotamuses, giraffes, and alligators use low-frequency sounds to communicate over long distances, often miles. Many animals also display wide-ranging emotions, including joy, happiness, empathy, compassion, grief, and even resentment and embarrassment. It's not surprising that animals share many emotions with us because we also share brain structures, located in the limbic system, that are the seat of our emotions.

options.label: A
options.text: Animals are more intelligent than us in sensing danger and detecting diseases.

options.label: B
options.text: The advanced sensory and motor abilities of animals is the reason why they can display wide- ranging emotions.

options.label: C
options.text: The similarity in brain structure explains why animals show emotions typically associated with humans.

options.label: D
options.text: Animals can show emotions which are typically associated with humans.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the main message is, not just any true statement.

The passage talks about animal abilities, but the key point comes at the end -> animals share emotions with humans because we have similar brain structures.

From passage: "It's not surprising that animals share many emotions with us because we also share brain structures, located in the limbic system, that are the seat of our emotions."

The thought process: Start with facts about animal abilities -> then emotions -> then explains why emotions exist -> shared brain structures. This explanation is the main point.

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> focuses only on disease detection, ignores the main point about emotions and brain structures completely

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> wrongly connects sensory abilities to emotions, but passage says emotions come from shared brain structures, not sensory skills

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> captures both the fact (animals show human emotions) and the scientific reason why (similar brain structures in limbic system)

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> states animals show emotions correctly, but completely misses the explanation of why this happens (brain structures), making it incomplete

The confusion many students have: Option 4 sounds right because it's true. But in summary questions, you need the complete picture, not just one true fact. Option 3 gives both the observation and the scientific explanation that ties the whole passage together.

questions.question_text: According to the text, the western barred bandicoots now have a flattering name because they have

options.label: A
options.text: led a revival in preserving the species.

options.label: B
options.text: led to a surge and increase of rainfall.

options.label: C
options.text: grown fivefold in terms of population.

options.label: D
options.text: aided in altering an arid environment.

questions.explanation_text:
Look for the "flattering name" mentioned in the passage -> need to find where this nickname appears and why they earned it.

From passage: "They have a new nickname—a flattering one, this time. 'We call them ecosystem engineers,' Pedler says."

The key is understanding why they're called "ecosystem engineers" -> look at the sentence right before this quote for the reason.

From passage: "With their constant digging, the bandicoots trap moisture and allow for seed germination so the cattle-damaged desert can restore itself."

Thought process: Flattering name = ecosystem engineers -> earned because they help fix/restore the damaged desert -> they dig constantly -> this traps water -> helps seeds grow -> desert heals itself.

🟠 Option 1 -> scope-error -> focuses on species revival, but the nickname is specifically about their environmental impact, not saving their own species

🔴 Option 2 -> reverses cause-effect -> passage says rainfall caused bandicoot population boom, not that bandicoots caused more rain - completely backwards

🟠 Option 3 -> context-shift -> population growth is mentioned but has nothing to do with why they got the flattering nickname "ecosystem engineers"

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> captures exactly why they earned the name "ecosystem engineers" - they alter the arid desert by trapping moisture and helping damaged land restore itself

questions.question_text: The text uses the word ‘exclosures’ because Wild Deserts has adopted a measure of

options.label: A
options.text: ridding the main desert of feral cats and large bilbies.

options.label: B
options.text: barring the entry of invasive species.

options.label: C
options.text: excluding animals to make the islands predator-free.

options.label: D
options.text: restoring cattle damaged deserts to green landscapes.

questions.explanation_text:
The question asks why the text uses the word 'exclosures' - we need to understand what these fenced areas are designed to do.

From passage: "The imported bandicoots occupy two fenced 'exclosures,' cleared of invasive rabbits (courtesy of Pedler's sheepdog) and of feral cats (which slunk off once the rabbits disappeared)."

Thought process: Look for definition -> exclosures are fenced areas -> cleared of invasive rabbits and cats -> purpose is to keep harmful animals OUT -> this means barring/excluding invasive species

Option analysis:

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> mentions feral cats correctly but says large bilbies are excluded, when passage shows bilbies are actually IN the Wild Training Zone, not excluded

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> perfectly matches what exclosures do - they're fenced areas that bar invasive rabbits and cats from entering

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> talks about making islands predator-free, but exclosures are on the mainland desert. The Shark Bay islands were already predator-free

🟠 Option 4 -> scope-error -> while bandicoots do help restore landscapes through digging, the exclosures' main job is to exclude invasive species, not directly restore green landscapes

Student confusion: You might think Option 4 sounds good because the passage mentions landscape restoration. But remember - the question asks why they use 'exclosures' specifically. These fenced areas are designed to keep bad animals OUT, not to restore landscapes directly.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following options does NOT represent the characteristics of the western barred bandicoot?

options.label: A
options.text: Shallow diggers having an elongated muzzle

options.label: B
options.text: Smallest black striped marsupial that uses camouflage and dig

options.label: C
options.text: Look of a rat but with a baby pouch and a slender snout

options.label: D
options.text: Long thin nose, black striped back, pouch for joeys

questions.explanation_text:
Look for what does NOT match the bandicoot's description means we need to find the option that has wrong or misleading information.

From passage: "They nicknamed one type the 'zebra rat' because of its black-striped rump... the zebra rat—the smallest bandicoot, more commonly known today as the western barred bandicoot"

From passage: "Their muzzle, which is much too long, gives them an air exceedingly stupid... It carried its breath-mint-size babies in a backward-facing pouch so mothers could forage for food and dig shallow, camouflaged shelters."

The key thinking process -> Find what the passage actually says about the bandicoot -> Compare each option against those facts -> Look for the one that doesn't match or adds wrong details.

🟢 Option 1 -> correct description -> passage clearly says "muzzle, which is much too long" (elongated) and "dig shallow, camouflaged shelters"

🔴 Option 2 -> scope-error -> calls it "smallest black striped marsupial" but passage only says it's the "smallest bandicoot" - this wrongly expands the comparison to all marsupials instead of just bandicoots

🟢 Option 3 -> correct description -> nicknamed "zebra rat", has "backward-facing pouch" for babies, and "muzzle, which is much too long" (slender snout)

🟢 Option 4 -> correct description -> "muzzle, which is much too long" (thin nose), "black-striped rump" (back), and "pouch" for babies

The confusion here might be thinking Option 2 sounds right because it mentions the correct features. But the tricky part is the phrase "smallest black striped marsupial" - the passage never compares it to other striped marsupials, only to other bandicoots.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements provides a gist of this passage?

options.label: A
options.text: The negligent attitude of the British colonists towards these bandicoots evidenced by the names given to them led to their annihilation.

options.label: B
options.text: A type of bandicoots was nearly wiped out by invasive species but rescuers now pin hopes on a remnant island population.

options.label: C
options.text: Marsupials are going extinct due to the colonial era transformation of the ecosystem which also destroyed natural vegetation.

options.label: D
options.text: The onslaught of animals, such as cattle, rabbits and housecats, brought in by the British led to the extinction of the western barred bandicoot.

questions.explanation_text:
Look for the main story here -> passage tells us about bandicoots surviving millions of years, then nearly going extinct due to invasive species, but now there's hope through island survivors being used for restoration.

From passage: "by the 1940s the western barred bandicoot, whose original range stretched across much of the continent, persisted only on two predator-free islands in Shark Bay" and "Now Wild Deserts is using descendants of those few thousand island survivors, called Shark Bay bandicoots, in a new effort to seed a mainland bandicoot revival."

Key story flow -> bandicoots survived 26 million years -> invasive species (cats, rabbits, cattle) nearly wiped them out -> only survived on islands -> now using island survivors for conservation -> some success happening.

🔴 Option 1 -> causation-error -> blames colonists' attitude and naming for bandicoot problems, but passage clearly shows invasive animals caused the damage, not names or attitudes

🟢 Option 2 -> captures main story accurately -> mentions "nearly wiped out by invasive species" ✓ and "hopes on remnant island population" ✓ -> perfect match for the conservation story

🟠 Option 3 -> scope-error -> talks about all marsupials when passage focuses specifically on bandicoots, also mentions vegetation destruction as main issue when it's really about predation

🟠 Option 4 -> degree-error -> says bandicoots went extinct but they actually survived on islands -> overstates the situation since there's an active restoration program using survivors

questions.question_text: In the first paragraph the author is making the point that economists like Becker

options.label: A
options.text: had begun to borrow concepts from other disciplines but were averse to the latter applying economic principles.

options.label: B
options.text: benefitted from the application of their principles and concepts to non-economic phenomena.

options.label: C
options.text: used economics to analyse non-market behaviour, without incorporating perspectives from other areas of inquiry.

options.label: D
options.text: tended to guard their discipline from poaching by academics from other subject areas.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to identify what point the author makes about economists like Becker.

The author describes Becker's approach in two parts: what he did and what he didn't do. This creates a contrast that's central to understanding the author's point.

From passage: "He projected economics outward into new realms: for example, by revealing the extent to which humans calculate marginal utilities when choosing their spouses or stealing from neighbors. At the same time, he did not let other ways of thinking enter his own economic realm: for example, he did not borrow from anthropology or history"

The thought process: Author shows Becker's one-way approach -> applies economics to other fields -> but refuses to learn from other fields -> this makes him "imperial"

🔴 Option 1 -> factual-error -> says Becker "borrowed concepts from other disciplines" but passage clearly states he did NOT borrow from anthropology or history

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> mentions applying economics to non-economic areas correctly, but misses the main criticism about refusing to incorporate other perspectives

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> captures both parts perfectly: used economics to analyze non-market behavior (YES) + without incorporating other perspectives (YES)

🟠 Option 4 -> scope-error -> focuses on "guarding from poaching" but the passage criticizes refusal to integrate insights, not fear of others using economic principles

The key confusion students face is between options 2 and 3. Option 2 sounds positive about Becker's approach, but the author is actually criticizing the one-sided nature. Option 3 captures this criticism by highlighting what Becker didn't do alongside what he did.

questions.question_text: “Times have changed for the once almighty discipline.” We can infer from this statement and the associated paragraph that the author is being

options.label: A
options.text: sarcastic about how economists, who earlier shunned other disciplines, are now beginning to incorporate them in their analyses.

options.label: B
options.text: critical of economists’ openly borrowing and collaborating across disciplines to explain how humans make decisions.

options.label: C
options.text: judgemental about the ability of economic tools to accurately manage crises leading to the downfall of this lofty science.

options.label: D
options.text: disparaging of economists’ inability to precisely predict market behaviour, and are now borrowing from other disciplines to remedy this.

questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace the author's thought process step by step:

Step 1: Author sets up contrast between past and present economics

  • Past: Gary Becker was "imperial" -> invaded other fields but didn't let others in
  • Present: economists are "reaching out, importing, borrowing"

Step 2: Look for tone clues in the language

  • "once almighty discipline" -> sounds mocking
  • "less imperial, more open" -> ironic about their change in attitude
  • The whole setup suggests the author finds it funny that proud economists now need help

From passage: "Economics has been taken to task, within and beyond its ramparts. Some economists have reached out, imported, borrowed, and collaborated—been less imperial, more open."

Thought Process: Author is highlighting irony -> economics used to be proud and invasive -> now they're humble and collaborative -> this shift is what the author finds amusing

Elimination Strategy: Look for what captures the ironic contrast between past arrogance and current humility.

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures the sarcastic tone about economists who once "shunned" other disciplines but now "incorporate them." This matches the imperial-to-collaborative shift perfectly.

🔴 Option 2 -> wrong direction -> says author is "critical of" the borrowing, but author isn't against the borrowing itself, just finds the change ironic.

🟠 Option 3 -> scope-error -> focuses on "crisis management" which isn't mentioned in this paragraph. The focus is on interdisciplinary approaches, not crisis handling.

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> mentions "predictive failures" but misses the main point about the ironic shift from imperial to collaborative attitudes.

The key is recognizing that the author finds it amusing (not critical) that formerly arrogant economists now need help from other fields.

questions.question_text: The author critiques Schiller's approach to behavioural economics for

options.label: A
options.text: denigrating the role of institutions while creating a link between behavioural economics and perceptions.

options.label: B
options.text: linking emotions and rational behaviour without considering the mediation of social institutions.

options.label: C
options.text: ignoring the marginal role that media and politics play in influencing people's behaviour.

options.label: D
options.text: relying excessively on storytelling as the main influence on the formation of perceptions.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find where the author specifically critiques Shiller's approach.

The key critique appears in the final paragraph where the author discusses what Shiller does and what he misses. The author explains Shiller's approach but then points out a major flaw.

From passage: "Yet institutions have been stripped from Shiller's account, to reveal a bare dynamic of emotions and economics, without the intermediating place of politics."

The thought process: Author says Shiller connects perceptions -> behavior -> social outcomes through storytelling. BUT the problem is institutions are missing -> this creates just emotions + economics -> without the mediating role of politics and institutions.

Elimination Process:

🔴 Option 1 -> misrepresents critique -> says Shiller "denigrates" institutions, but passage shows he simply omits them, not attacks them

🟢 Option 2 -> captures exact critique -> Shiller links emotions/behavior but strips out institutions that should mediate this process

🔴 Option 3 -> contradicts passage -> calls media/politics "marginal" when passage says they play "vital role" in mediating interests

🔴 Option 4 -> wrong focus -> passage doesn't criticize storytelling itself, but rather the missing institutional framework

The confusion students might have: Options 1 and 2 both mention institutions. But option 1 says Shiller actively attacks institutions while option 2 says he simply ignores their mediating role. The passage shows Shiller just left them out of his model, not that he deliberately criticized them.

questions.question_text: We can infer from the passage that the term “homo economic us" refers to someone

options.label: A
options.text: maximises their opportunities based on nonmarket choices.

options.label: B
options.text: makes rational decisions based on their own preferences.

options.label: C
options.text: believes in borrowing and collaborating with other disciplines in their work.

options.label: D
options.text: is not influenced by the preferences and choices of others.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "For generations, economists have presumed that people have interests—'preferences,' in the neoclassical argot—that get revealed in the course of peoples' choices. Interests come before actions and determine them."

From passage: "even some mainstream economists have to admit that homo economicus doesn't always behave like the textbook maximizer"

The passage shows homo economicus as the traditional economic model -> people make calculated choices based on their preferences -> these preferences drive their actions -> they act as "textbook maximizers" who reveal preferences through rational choices.

🔴 Option 1 -> context-shift -> says "nonmarket choices" but homo economicus is about market-like rational thinking applied everywhere, not specifically nonmarket behavior

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> perfectly matches the passage's core description of rational decision-making driven by individual preferences and maximizing behavior

🔴 Option 3 -> opposite-meaning -> the passage shows Becker as homo economicus specifically not borrowing from other disciplines - this contradicts the concept entirely

🟠 Option 4 -> too-narrow -> while homo economicus focuses on individual preferences, this misses the main point about rational preference-based decision making which is the core concept

The passage clearly defines homo economicus through the preference-choice relationship and rational maximizing behavior, making Option 2 the direct match.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. Animals have an interest in fulfilling their basic needs, but also in avoiding suffering, and thus we ought to extend moral consideration.
  2. Singer viewed himself as a utilitarian, and presents a direct moral theory concerning animal rights, in contrast to indirect positions, such as welfarist views.
  3. He argued for extending moral consideration to animals because, similar to humans, animals have certain significant interests.
  4. The event that publicly announced animal rights as a legitimate issue within contemporary philosophy was Peter Singer's Animal Liberation text in 1975.
  5. As such, we ought to view their interests alongside and equal to human interests, which results in humans having direct moral duties towards animals.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Find the main topic -> Most sentences mention Singer specifically, so this passage is about Singer's philosophy, not just general animal rights.

Step 2: Look for the flow -> We need sentences that connect Singer's ideas in a logical order.

From passage: "Singer viewed himself as a utilitarian, and presents a direct moral theory" and "He argued for extending moral consideration to animals"

The word "He" in sentence 3 clearly refers back to Singer from sentence 2. This shows these sentences connect.

Step 3: Check each sentence's focus -> Does it talk about Singer specifically or just general ideas?

Sentences 2, 3, 4, 5 all mention Singer or refer to him with "He" -> they form a connected story

Sentence 1 talks about animals in general -> doesn't mention Singer

Analysis:

🔴 Sentence 1 -> scope-error -> This is a general statement about animals having needs and deserving moral consideration. While true, it doesn't connect to Singer's specific argument that the other sentences discuss. It's like starting a story about Shakespeare but then talking about poetry in general.

🟢 Sentences 2, 3, 4, 5 -> These form a complete story: Singer's background (sentence 2) -> his argument (sentence 3) -> historical context (sentence 4) -> conclusion (sentence 5). They all focus specifically on Singer's philosophy.

Answer: 1

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Certain codes may, of course, be so widely distributed in a specific language community or culture, and be learned at so early an age, that they appear not to be constructed – the effect of an articulation between sign and referent – but to be 'naturally' given. Simple visual signs appear to have achieved a 'near-universality' in this sense: though evidence remains that even apparently 'natural' visual codes are culture specific. However, this does not mean that no codes have intervened; rather, that the codes have been profoundly naturalized. The operation of naturalized codes reveals not the transparency and 'naturalness' of language but the depth, the habituation and the near-universality of the codes in use. They produce apparently 'natural' recognitions. This has the (ideological) effect of concealing the practices of coding which are present.

options.label: A
options.text: All codes, linguistic and visual, have a natural origin but some are so widespread that they become universal. This is what hides the mechanism of coding behind signs.

options.label: B
options.text: Learning linguistic and visual signs at an early age makes all such codes appear natural. This naturalization of codes is the effect of ideology.

options.label: C
options.text: Not all codes are natural but certain codes are naturalized and made to appear universal. Ideology aims to hide the mechanism of coding behind signs.

options.label: D
options.text: Language and visual signs are codes. However, some of the codes are so widespread that they not only seem naturally given but also hide the mechanism of coding behind the signs.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage talks about how some codes become so common that they seem natural instead of made by people. The key is understanding that these codes aren't really natural - they just appear natural because we use them so much.

From passage: "Certain codes may, of course, be so widely distributed in a specific language community or culture, and be learned at so early an age, that they appear not to be constructed – the effect of an articulation between sign and referent – but to be 'naturally' given."

Think process: Codes are everywhere -> we learn them early -> they feel natural -> but they're still made by people -> this hides the fact that they're constructed.

Option elimination strategy: Look for the option that gets both parts right: (1) codes seem natural but aren't really, and (2) this appearance hides the coding process.

🔴 Option 1 -> inaccurate -> says codes "have a natural origin" but passage says they only appear natural while being culture-specific

🟠 Option 2 -> scope-error -> only focuses on "early age learning" but ignores "widespread distribution." Also gets causation backwards - says naturalization is effect of ideology instead of naturalization having ideological effect

🟠 Option 3 -> degree-error -> right direction but overstates ideology's role. Says "ideology aims to hide" but passage only says naturalization "has the (ideological) effect of concealing" - describes result, not purpose

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> captures both key ideas: codes are widespread and seem naturally given (not actually natural) + this appearance hides the coding mechanism. No overstatement about ideology's aims.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. Urbanites also have more and better options for getting around: Uber is ubiquitous; easy-to-rent dockless bicycles are spreading; battery-powered scooters will be next.
  2. When more people use buses or trains the service usually improves because public-transport agencies run more buses and trains.
  3. Worsening services on public transport, terrorist attacks in some urban metros and a rise in fares have been blamed for this trend.
  4. It seems more likely that public transport is being squeezed structurally as people's need to travel is diminishing as a result of smartphones, video-conferencing, online shopping and so on.
  5. There has been a puzzling decline in the use of urban public transport in many countries in the west, despite the growth in urban populations and rising employment.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Find the main topic -> Sentence 5 talks about a "puzzling decline in the use of urban public transport" - this sets up the whole discussion.

Step 2: Look for sentences that explain this decline or connect to it -> Sentences 3 and 4 both give reasons for the decline. Sentence 1 mentions alternatives people now have.

Step 3: Check which sentence goes against the flow -> Sentence 2 talks about improvement when more people use public transport, but the whole passage is about fewer people using it.

From passage: "There has been a puzzling decline in the use of urban public transport in many countries in the west, despite the growth in urban populations and rising employment."

Thought process: Main topic is decline in public transport use -> Sentences 3 & 4 explain why decline happens -> Sentence 1 shows what alternatives people have instead -> But sentence 2 talks about services getting better when more people use transport, which contradicts the whole "decline" theme.

Logical flow of four sentences:

  • Sentence 5: Sets up the puzzle (decline in public transport)
  • Sentence 3: First explanation (bad services, attacks, high fares)
  • Sentence 4: Better explanation (technology reducing need to travel)
  • Sentence 1: Shows alternatives available (Uber, bikes, scooters)

The odd one out: Sentence 2 discusses improvement in public transport when usage increases, but the entire passage focuses on decreasing usage and its causes. This sentence doesn't fit the theme at all.

Answer: 2

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: ___ (1) ___ You can't just put things anywhere you want to. The evolved architecture of the brain is haphazard and disjointed, and incorporates multiple systems, each of which has a mind of its own ___ (2) ___ . questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "You can't just put things anywhere you want to. The evolved architecture of the brain is haphazard and disjointed"

The sentence compares brain organization -> home office organization. This sets up a contrast -> the brain is NOT organized like things we organize carefully.

Thought process: Introduction sentence -> should come first to set up the main idea -> then paragraph explains WHY the brain isn't organized that way (evolution, no planner, etc.)

🟠 Option 1 (Position 3): degree-error -> sentence talks about basic organization, but position 3 is deep into evolution discussion. Wrong timing in the flow.

🟢 Option 2 (Position 1): perfect fit -> introduces the contrast theme right away, then rest of paragraph explains why brain isn't organized like our stuff.

🟠 Option 3 (Position 2): context-shift -> interrupts the flow between "can't put things anywhere" and "evolved architecture." Breaks the natural connection.

🟠 Option 4 (Position 4): scope-error -> paragraph ends with strong house metaphor. Adding this sentence after would weaken that powerful ending.

The sentence needs to introduce the contrast idea, not interrupt or conclude it.

These countries lie at the centre of global affairs: they have since the beginning of history. Running across the spine of Asia, they form a web of connections fanning out in every direction, routes along which pilgrims and warriors, nomads and merchants have travelled, goods and produce have been bought and sold, and ideas exchanged, adapted and refined ___ (2) ___ . They have carried not only prosperity, but also death and violence, disease and disaster ___ (3) ___ . The Silk Roads are the world's central nervous system, connecting otherwise far-flung peoples and places ___ (4) ___ . It allows us to see patterns and links, causes and effects that remain invisible if one looks only at Europe, or North America.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "The Silk Roads are the world's central nervous system, connecting otherwise far-flung peoples and places"

The key is to follow the logical flow -> the paragraph moves from describing these countries -> their historical connections -> their impact (both good and bad) -> their role as a central nervous system.

The sentence we need to place talks about understanding this role and how it helps us see global connections. This sounds like a conclusion that builds on the main idea.

Many students might think blank 2 works because it mentions connections and routes. But that section is still describing the historical activities, not the broader understanding we gain.

Others might consider blank 3 since it mentions global impact, but that section focuses on negative effects (death, disease), while our sentence has a positive, analytical tone.

🔴 Option 1 (Blank 1) -> context-shift -> comes right after "disrepair" which is negative, but our sentence is about understanding benefits - doesn't flow logically

🟠 Option 3 (Blank 2) -> premature -> this section is still listing activities (pilgrims, merchants, etc.) but hasn't yet made the big picture point our sentence addresses

🟠 Option 4 (Blank 3) -> tone-mismatch -> this section focuses on death and violence, but our sentence is about positive understanding - jarring transition

🟢 Option 2 (Blank 4) -> perfect flow -> comes after the central nervous system metaphor, and our sentence explains why this matters - it helps us understand global patterns
